The Adventures of Tom Sawyer was written by Mark Twain and first published in 1876. It captures the freedom, mischief and adventure of boyhood along the great Mississippi River in old America. Mark Twain drew on memories of his own childhood to create Tom, one of the most famous and beloved boys in all of literature. This retelling keeps his spirit for young readers.

Tom Sawyer was a lively, mischievous boy who lived long ago in a small town beside the great Mississippi River. He was raised by his kind but strict Aunt Polly, and he was forever getting into scrapes, dodging school, and dreaming up adventures. He was clever, brave, and a great deal of trouble, and everybody in town knew his name.

image.note: A grinning barefoot boy in old clothes by a wide sunny river; a small riverside town behind; lively, mischievous

pages.text: One Saturday, as a punishment for skipping school and coming home muddy, Aunt Polly ordered Tom to whitewash the whole long fence. It was a huge, boring job on a beautiful sunny day, just when every other boy was off to play. Tom stared gloomily at the endless fence and felt the misery of the whole afternoon stretching out before him.

image.note: Tom scowling at a very long fence with a bucket of whitewash, other boys running off to play in the sun; glum

pages.text: But Tom was clever. When another boy came by to tease him, Tom pretended that whitewashing was a rare and wonderful treat, an honour that few boys were ever allowed. He brushed away with such joy and pride that the other boy grew envious, and soon begged for a turn. Tom, acting reluctant, generously allowed it, for a small payment.

image.note: Tom painting with exaggerated delight; another boy watching, growing envious; sly, comic

pages.text: The trick worked marvellously. Before long, boys were queuing up and handing over their treasures, an apple, a marble, a kite, just for the privilege of doing Tom's work for him. By the afternoon, the fence had three coats of whitewash, Tom had not lifted a finger, and his pockets were full of riches. He had learned a sly truth: to make a boy want a thing, just make it hard to get.

image.note: A whole line of boys eagerly whitewashing the fence, handing Tom their treasures; Tom lounging, pockets full; triumphant

pages.text: Tom's best friend was Huckleberry Finn, a ragged, carefree boy who answered to no one and did just as he pleased. Every boy in town secretly envied Huck's freedom. Together, Tom, Huck and another friend hatched a grand plan. They would run away to a wooded island in the middle of the great river, and there they would live wild and free as pirates.

image.note: Tom with the ragged, free-spirited Huck Finn; the two boys plotting adventure; a wooded river island beyond

pages.text: One night the boys crept out, took a raft, and paddled to the island. For days they lived a glorious life, swimming, fishing, roasting their catch over a fire, and lazing in the sun with no grown-up to tell them what to do. It was everything they had dreamed. And yet, as the days passed, Tom began to feel a small, surprising tug in his chest: he was homesick.

image.note: Three boys living happily on an island: a campfire, fishing, swimming; free and sunburnt; idyllic

pages.text: Back in town, everyone believed the boys had drowned in the river. The whole town was plunged into mourning. Tom, sneaking home in secret one night to spy, overheard the sad news and had a wonderfully wicked idea. He raced back to tell his friends. They would stay hidden just a little longer, and then make the grandest, most dramatic return any boy ever made.

image.note: Tom hidden in shadow, overhearing the mournful townsfolk who think the boys are dead; a mischievous idea forming

pages.text: On the day the town gathered in church to mourn the three lost boys, the doors swung open, and in they marched, alive and grinning. The whole congregation gasped, then wept, then laughed for joy. Aunt Polly hugged Tom so hard he could scarcely breathe. It was the most magnificent moment of Tom's whole life, to attend his very own funeral.

image.note: The three "drowned" boys strolling alive into their own funeral service; the congregation astonished and overjoyed

pages.text: But not all of Tom's adventures were merry. One night, he and Huck had crept into the graveyard on a dare, and there, hidden and terrified, they had secretly witnessed a wicked man named Injun Joe commit a dreadful crime and blame it on an innocent person. The boys were petrified, and swore each other to secrecy, for they feared the dangerous villain would come after them if he knew.

image.note: Two frightened boys hiding behind gravestones at night, witnessing a shadowy crime; fearful, tense; not gory

pages.text: When the innocent man was put on trial for the crime, Tom's conscience would not let him stay silent, though he was terrified. Bravely, he stood up in the crowded courtroom and told the truth of what he had seen. The innocent man was freed, but the real villain leapt up and escaped before he could be caught, and vanished. Now the dangerous man had good reason to hate Tom.

image.note: Tom standing up bravely in a courtroom to tell the truth; the villain leaping away to escape; courage and danger

pages.text: Some time later, Tom and a girl from town were exploring a huge, winding cave during a picnic, and wandered too far. To their horror, they realised they were completely lost in the dark maze of tunnels, with their candles burning low. For days their families searched frantically, while the two children, hungry and frightened, tried desperately to find their way out.

image.note: Tom and a girl lost in a vast dark cave, holding a guttering candle; endless tunnels; frightening but hopeful

pages.text: Worse still, deep in the cave, Tom suddenly glimpsed the very villain, Injun Joe, who was hiding there. Tom's heart nearly stopped. But keeping his wits, Tom kept the girl calm, and searched on bravely until, at last, far off, he spied a tiny speck of daylight. Following it, the exhausted children found a way out and were joyfully reunited with their frantic families.

image.note: Tom spotting a distant pinprick of daylight in the dark cave, leading the girl toward it; relief, escape

pages.text: The cave was then sealed shut for safety, and the villain, trapped inside, met his end there, so that Tom and Huck were finally safe from him. And Tom, remembering the villain had been hiding treasure, led Huck back to the cave. There, in a secret spot, the two boys uncovered a real hidden box of gold coins, a fortune, all their own.

image.note: Tom and Huck lifting a heavy box of gold coins from a hidden nook in the cave; wide-eyed wonder; treasure at last

pages.text: And so Tom Sawyer's adventures ended in real riches, real courage, and a fame that spread all through the town. He had played pirates, attended his own funeral, saved an innocent man, escaped a villain, and found buried gold, all before he was even grown. Not bad, thought Tom happily, for a boy who had only wanted to skip whitewashing a fence.

image.note: Tom and Huck grinning with their treasure, the sunny river town behind them; adventure rewarded; closing, warm
